sections.heading: Typical Permanent Christmas Light Prices in Ontario for 2026
paragraphs: For a professionally installed permanent LED system in Southwestern Ontario, most projects land between $2,500 and $8,000. A modest bungalow in Woodstock or Ingersoll with only the front roofline lit sits near the lower end, while a two-storey home in London or Kitchener-Waterloo with full wraparound coverage, multiple gables and a detached garage moves toward the upper end. These are realistic estimates, not fixed quotes, because no two rooflines are quite the same.

The table below groups typical Ontario homes by lit roofline length. Most homes in our service area have between 100 and 250 linear feet of usable soffit or fascia once you add up the front, sides and back. Many homeowners start with the front and the sides that face the street, then add the rear or a garage later, since the system can be extended with matching track and the same app.

sections.heading: What Drives the Cost of Permanent Roofline Lighting
paragraphs: Linear footage is the single biggest factor, since every foot needs aluminum track, LEDs and cable. After that, complexity matters. A simple rectangular roofline with long straight runs installs quickly, while a home with steep peaks, inside and outside corners, multiple elevations and short broken runs takes more labour and more connectors. Height also plays a role: a three-storey rear elevation or a walkout basement side may need extra ladder work or staging.

Zones and power placement add smaller amounts. If you want the front, the garage and the backyard to run different scenes, each zone needs its own data run. The controller usually plugs into an exterior GFCI outlet, so if there is no outlet near where the system starts, a licensed electrician may need to add one, which falls under the Ontario Electrical Safety Code and an ESA permit.

Ask whether the warranty is part of the price or an add-on. Our systems carry a lifetime warranty on parts, hardware and workmanship, so there is no separate service plan to buy. Be cautious of low quotes that leave out the controller, charge extra for colour-matching, or price the LEDs alone and treat installation as a separate line. Compare total installed price per lit foot, not just the headline number.

sections.heading: Permanent Lights vs Paying for Seasonal Installation Every Year
paragraphs: Many Ontario homeowners already pay a company to hang Christmas lights each fall and take them down in January. Industry pricing for that service on an average home commonly runs several hundred to over a thousand dollars per season, depending on size and whether lights are rented. That cost repeats every year and only covers one holiday, whereas a permanent system can run Halloween, Canada Day, game nights and everyday white accent lighting.

Using rough numbers, a $4,500 permanent system compared against $800 per year for seasonal installation breaks even in a little under six years. If you were spending more, or you value the year-round use, the payback is faster. If you have never paid for installation and hang lights yourself, the value is less about dollars and more about safety, time and getting off the ladder for good.

sections.heading: Ways to Manage Your Budget Without Cutting Quality
paragraphs: The most effective way to control cost is to phase the project. Light the front elevation and the street-facing side first, which is where most of the visual impact lives, then add the back or garage in a later season. Because the track is colour-matched and controlled from one app, an addition looks like it was always part of the original install, provided the same system is used.

Booking outside the October and November rush can also help with scheduling flexibility, and spring or summer installs are common since the lights are useful year-round. What we do not recommend is dropping to cheaper non-addressable strips or skipping colour-matched track. Those savings tend to show up later as a visible eyesore in daylight or a system that cannot do the scenes you actually wanted.

title: Permanent LED Lights vs Seasonal Christmas Lights: Which Is Right?
metaDescription: Permanent LED lights vs seasonal Christmas lights in Ontario: compare cost, looks, daytime visibility, winter durability and year-round use to choose well.
summary: Permanent LED lights suit homeowners who want year-round, app-controlled lighting for every holiday with no annual ladder work, while seasonal C9 Christmas lights suit those who love the classic big-bulb look mainly for the Christmas season. The right choice depends on how long you plan to stay in the home, how often you want lighting beyond December, and whether you prefer a one-time investment or a yearly service.
keyTakeaways: Permanent systems are a one-time investment, typically $2,500 to $8,000 in Ontario, while seasonal installation is a recurring yearly cost.
Seasonal C9 lights deliver the traditional warm, chunky-bulb Christmas look that many people associate with the holidays.
Permanent RGBW LEDs can show 16 million plus colours and run scenes for every holiday, plus everyday white accent lighting.
Colour-matched permanent track sits nearly invisible in daylight, whereas seasonal clips and wires are visible until takedown in January.
Many homeowners choose seasonal C9 if they may move within a few years and permanent if they plan to stay.

sections.heading: Permanent vs Seasonal Christmas Lights at a Glance
paragraphs: Both options put light on your roofline, but they work very differently. Permanent lighting is aluminum track colour-matched to your soffit or fascia with individually addressable RGBW LEDs, controlled by an app and left in place all year. Seasonal C9 lighting is the classic big-bulb string clipped along the eaves in October or November and removed in January, either rented or purchased.

The comparison below sums up the practical differences homeowners in London, Kitchener-Waterloo, Woodstock and the rest of Southwestern Ontario ask about most. Cost figures are estimates, and seasonal pricing varies widely between companies and home sizes. Use it as a starting point, then weigh the factors that matter most to your household, such as how long you plan to stay, how much you decorate beyond December, and whether you would rather pay once or budget for a service every fall.

sections.heading: The Look: Classic C9 Glow vs Programmable RGBW
paragraphs: There is a real aesthetic difference. C9 bulbs are large, rounded and spaced evenly, producing the warm, nostalgic outline many people picture when they think of a Christmas house. They read clearly from the street and look especially good on traditional brick homes and farmhouses in towns like Stratford and Ingersoll. If that specific look is what you love, nothing quite replicates it.

Permanent LEDs are smaller points of light that sit inside a channel. Their strength is flexibility: warm white that closely mimics a classic string, a red and green alternating pattern, a slow twinkle, or a full colour chase for a party. Each LED is individually addressable, so you can create patterns that strings of fixed bulbs cannot. Some homeowners even run both, using permanent track for year-round use and C9 accents on trees or railings.

sections.heading: Cost Over Five and Ten Years
paragraphs: Seasonal installation looks cheaper in the first year because you are paying for one season of labour and rental. The difference is that the bill comes back every autumn. If professional installation on your home costs roughly $700 to $1,200 a season, which is a common estimate for a mid-sized Ontario home, five years adds up to $3,500 to $6,000 and ten years doubles that.

A permanent system front-loads the cost and then mostly stops. Electricity for LED scenes is modest, the lifetime warranty covers parts, hardware and workmanship, and there is no annual install fee. Over a five-year horizon the two options are often close. Beyond that, permanent lighting usually comes out ahead, which is why the length of time you expect to stay in the home matters so much.

sections.heading: Convenience, Safety and Ontario Weather
paragraphs: Hanging lights in Ontario usually happens in cold, wet, windy weather, and takedown in January can mean ice on the eaves and frozen clips. Seasonal professional service removes that risk from you, but the work still has to be scheduled around the weather and booked early, since October and November fill up fast. Our early-bird booking closes September 30 for that reason.

Permanent lighting is a single install that can happen in any season. Once it is up, there is no ladder work at all. The track and LEDs are IP67 sealed, cold-rated to minus 40 degrees Celsius and use UV-rated cable, so they handle lake-effect snow, freeze-thaw cycles and summer sun without being taken down. Brightness and scenes are changed from your phone, so there is never a reason to climb up after a storm to fix a sagging strand or a burnt-out bulb.

sections.heading: Year-Round Use Beyond Christmas
paragraphs: The biggest functional difference is how many days of the year the lights earn their keep. Seasonal C9 lights shine for six to ten weeks. Permanent systems run warm white accent lighting on ordinary evenings, orange and purple for Halloween, red and white for Canada Day, team colours on game day and soft pastels for Easter or a birthday. The same hardware that delivers Christmas also covers every other occasion.

Many owners end up using permanent lights more for everyday curb appeal and security than for Christmas. A schedule can turn on warm white at dusk and switch off at midnight every night, which lights the driveway and entry while giving the house a finished, architectural look. Because the lights are sealed in track and scheduled in the app, that everyday use takes no effort at all. Seasonal strings, by contrast, are designed and priced for a short holiday window and are not meant to stay up through spring and summer.

sections.heading: Which Option Should You Choose?
paragraphs: Choose seasonal C9 lights if you love the traditional big-bulb look, mainly decorate for Christmas, rent your home or may move within a few years, or simply want to try professional lighting before committing. Renting the lights keeps the upfront cost lowest, while buying them makes sense if you plan to use the same set for several seasons. Early-bird booking before September 30 secures the best install dates.

Choose permanent lighting if you plan to stay for the long term, want lighting for multiple holidays and everyday use, prefer a clean daytime appearance and never want to book a seasonal install again. If you are unsure, book a free on-site demo: we light a sample section on your actual house at night so you can judge it in person.

faqs.question: Are permanent lights as bright as C9 Christmas lights?
faqs.answer: They are bright, but the effect is different. C9 bulbs are large and diffused, so each bulb reads as a soft glowing point. Permanent LEDs are smaller and more numerous, and brightness is adjustable in the app. Most homeowners run permanent lights below full brightness for a refined look, with plenty of headroom for festive occasions.

faqs.question: Can permanent lights look like traditional warm white Christmas lights?
faqs.answer: Yes. RGBW LEDs include a dedicated white channel, so warm white scenes look natural rather than tinted. You can save a warm white Christmas scene, a red and green pattern or a classic multicolour look and schedule them for December. The main visual difference from C9 is bulb size and spacing.

faqs.question: Is it worth installing permanent lights if I might move?
faqs.answer: If you expect to move within two or three years, seasonal C9 service is often the better value. If you plan to stay five years or more, permanent lighting usually costs less over time and adds curb appeal that buyers notice when you eventually sell.

title: How Permanent Roofline Lighting Works: Track, LEDs, Controller, App
metaDescription: How permanent roofline lighting works on Ontario homes: colour-matched aluminum track, addressable RGBW LEDs, the controller, power supply and phone app.
summary: Permanent roofline lighting uses a slim aluminum track, colour-matched to your soffit or fascia, that holds a run of individually addressable RGBW LEDs connected to a weatherproof controller and power supply. The controller talks to an app on your phone, which lets you pick colours, run scenes and animations, set schedules and split the house into zones.
keyTakeaways: The aluminum track is painted to match your soffit or fascia and clips into the soffit or fascia channel with no roof penetration.
Each RGBW LED is individually addressable, so every point of light can be a different colour or brightness.
A low-voltage power supply and controller usually plug into an exterior GFCI outlet and send data along the LED run.
The app stores scenes, schedules, timers and zones, so the lights run automatically once set up.
Components are IP67 sealed, cold-rated to minus 40 degrees Celsius and rated for 50,000 plus hours of LED life.

sections.heading: The Four Parts of a Permanent Lighting System
paragraphs: Every permanent roofline system has four main components working together. The track is the visible housing along your roofline. The LEDs sit inside the track and produce the light. The power supply converts household power into the low voltage the LEDs need. The controller is the brain, translating what you choose in the app into data that tells each LED what to do.

Understanding these parts helps you compare quotes. Two systems can look identical from the street on installation day but differ in track quality, LED density, weather sealing and how capable the app is. Those differences show up years later in how well the lights hold colour, how they look in daylight and how easy they are to use. A good installer will explain each part plainly.
bullets: Track: aluminum channel, colour-matched to soffit or fascia
LEDs: individually addressable RGBW nodes, IP67 sealed
Power supply: converts 120V household power to safe low voltage
Controller and app: stores scenes, schedules, zones and timers

sections.heading: The Aluminum Track and Colour-Matching
paragraphs: The track is a slim aluminum profile that runs along the underside of the soffit or the face of the fascia, following the roofline around corners and up peaks. It protects the LEDs from snow, ice and sun, and it gives the installation a straight, finished line. Because it is aluminum rather than plastic, it will not sag or become brittle after years of Ontario temperature swings.

We colour-match the track to your existing soffit or fascia, whether that is white, black, brown, grey or a less common shade. When the lights are off, the track blends into the trim and is hard to notice from the street. Installation uses the soffit or fascia channel itself, so nothing goes through the shingles or roof deck. That protects your roofing warranty.

sections.heading: Individually Addressable RGBW LEDs Explained
paragraphs: RGBW stands for red, green, blue and white. Mixing red, green and blue produces more than 16 million colours, while the dedicated white channel gives a clean, natural white instead of the slightly bluish white you get by mixing RGB alone. That white channel is what makes everyday accent lighting and warm white Christmas scenes look right. It is the W in RGBW that earns its keep daily.

Individually addressable means each LED node has its own tiny chip and can be told to show a different colour and brightness from its neighbours. That is what allows chases, twinkles, gradients, alternating holiday patterns and precise spotlighting of doors or peaks. Non-addressable strips can only show one colour along the whole run, which limits what you can do. Rated LED life is 50,000 plus hours.

sections.heading: Power Supply, Controller and Wiring
paragraphs: Household current runs at 120 volts, but LEDs operate on low voltage. A weatherproof power supply handles that conversion, usually mounted in a protected location near an exterior outlet, in the garage or in the attic space. For longer rooflines, power may be injected at more than one point so colours stay consistent from one end to the other. This is planned during the quote.

The controller connects to your home Wi-Fi and sends data down the LED run. Most installations simply plug into an existing exterior GFCI outlet. If an outlet needs to be added or a dedicated circuit is preferred, that work should be done by a licensed electrical contractor under the Ontario Electrical Safety Code, with an Electrical Safety Authority (ESA) notification of work. Cabling between sections is UV-rated and routed tidily along the trim.

sections.heading: How the App Controls Your Lights
paragraphs: Once the system is online, the app becomes your control panel. You can choose a solid colour, pick from saved holiday scenes, build your own patterns, adjust brightness and speed, and turn zones on or off independently. Changes happen within a second or two, so you can try ideas from the driveway and see the result immediately. Brightness can be fine-tuned the same way.

Schedules are where the system really saves effort. You can set warm white to come on at sunset every day, switch to a Halloween scene for the last week of October and run a Christmas pattern from December 1 to January 6. After that, the lights largely run themselves. During our install, we set up starter scenes and schedules and walk you through the app before we leave.

sections.heading: What Happens on Installation Day
paragraphs: Most residential installs take one to two days. The crew confirms the layout and zones with you, mounts the colour-matched track along the planned runs, seats the LEDs, routes power and data cable, and installs the power supply and controller. Each run is tested section by section so any issue is caught before the crew packs up. The work area is tidied before the crew leaves.

Before booking, we offer a free on-site demo where we colour-match your soffit, mount a live sample section and light it at night. That lets you see the brightness, the LED spacing and how the track looks against your trim, so there are no surprises when the full system goes up. It is free, and there is no obligation to buy if the look is not right for your home.

faqs.question: Do permanent lights need a separate electrical circuit?
faqs.answer: Usually not. A typical residential system plugs into an existing exterior GFCI outlet because LED power draw is low. If there is no outlet nearby or you want a dedicated circuit, a licensed electrical contractor should do that work under the Ontario Electrical Safety Code with an ESA notification.

faqs.question: What happens if the Wi-Fi goes down?
faqs.answer: Saved schedules typically live on the controller itself, so the lights keep following their programmed routine even if the internet drops. You will not be able to change scenes remotely until the connection returns, but the system does not simply stop working because of a brief outage.

faqs.question: Can one LED be replaced if it fails?
faqs.answer: Yes. Because the system is modular and housed in track, an individual section can be swapped without removing the whole run. Failures are uncommon given the 50,000 plus hour rated life, and replacement parts and labour are covered by our lifetime warranty.

faqs.question: Do I need to drill into my roof?
faqs.answer: No. The track mounts to the soffit or fascia channel, not through shingles or the roof deck. That avoids creating leak points and keeps your roofing warranty intact. Your shingles, underlayment and roof deck are left untouched. It also means installation is quicker and the lights can be removed later without leaving holes in the roof.

title: Are Permanent Holiday Lights Visible During the Day?
metaTitle: Are Permanent Lights Visible During the Day?
metaDescription: Are permanent holiday lights visible during the day? How colour-matched track hides permanent LED lighting on Ontario homes, and what you see up close.
summary: When properly installed in colour-matched track, permanent holiday lights are very hard to see during the day from the street, because the slim aluminum channel blends into your soffit or fascia like part of the trim. Up close or from directly below you can see the track and the small LED lenses, but there are no hanging wires, clips or bulbs like seasonal lights.
keyTakeaways: Colour-matched aluminum track is the main reason permanent lights disappear into the roofline in daylight.
From typical street distance the track reads as part of the trim; from directly beneath it is visible but tidy.
Placement on the soffit underside versus the fascia face changes how visible the system is.
Poorly matched track, loose cable and uneven runs are what make some installs look obvious during the day.
A free on-site demo lets you check daytime and night-time appearance on your own house before committing.

sections.heading: Why Colour-Matched Track Makes Lights Nearly Invisible
paragraphs: Your eye picks out contrast, not objects. A white plastic clip on brown fascia or a green wire against white soffit stands out immediately. A slim aluminum channel finished in the same colour as the trim it sits on has almost no contrast, so from the sidewalk or across the street it reads as part of the house rather than something added to it.

That is why we colour-match the track to your existing soffit or fascia rather than offering one or two stock colours. Ontario subdivisions use a wide range of trim colours, from bright white and almond to charcoal, black, brown and various greys. Matching closely is the single most important factor in how the system looks for the 300 or so days a year it is not putting on a show.

sections.heading: What You See From the Street vs Up Close
paragraphs: From a typical viewing distance, such as the road, a neighbour's driveway or a real estate listing photo, a well-installed system is very difficult to spot. Most people cannot tell a house has permanent lights until they come on at dusk. That is a big difference from seasonal lights, which remain visible as clips and strings from installation in the fall until removal in January.

Standing on your front step and looking straight up is different. From there you can see the track running along the soffit and the small LED lenses at regular spacing. It looks tidy and intentional, a bit like low-profile trim or under-cabinet lighting, but it is not invisible. Setting expectations honestly here avoids disappointment later. It also means you should judge the system from where people actually see your home.

sections.heading: Soffit vs Fascia Placement and Daytime Visibility
paragraphs: Where the track is mounted changes how much of it you see. Mounting on the underside of the soffit, tucked toward the outer edge, hides the system best from street level because you are looking at the house from below and to the side. The light still washes outward and down, outlining the roofline clearly at night. It also keeps the track out of direct sun.

Fascia-face mounting can be the better choice when soffits are shallow, when there is a gutter design that blocks light, or when the homeowner wants a crisper outline at night. It is somewhat more visible during the day, which makes colour-matching even more important. During the demo we can show both positions so you can decide based on your own house rather than a brochure photo.

sections.heading: Installation Details That Keep Lights Discreet
paragraphs: Colour is only part of a clean daytime look. Straight, level runs matter, since a track that wanders or dips catches the eye even when it matches. Corners and peaks should be mitred or joined neatly. Power and data cable should be routed along trim lines or inside the track rather than looped across siding, and the controller and power supply should be placed somewhere protected and out of sight.

Many of the permanent lighting installs that look obvious in daylight have one of a few common problems: generic white track on dark trim, cable zip-tied to gutters, or visible end caps and gaps between sections. When comparing installers, ask to see daytime photos of past jobs, not just night shots. Daylight photos reveal far more about the quality of an installation than any glowing night shot can.
bullets: Track colour-matched to the actual trim, not a near match
Straight, level runs with neat corners and peaks
Cable hidden in the track or along trim lines
Controller and power supply mounted out of sight

Using warm white for everyday accent lighting and saving bright colour shows for holidays keeps the house looking refined rather than flashy, and brightness can be reduced in the app at any time. title: Can Permanent Outdoor Lights Survive Ontario Winters?
metaTitle: Permanent Outdoor Lights in Ontario Winters
metaDescription: Can permanent outdoor lights survive Ontario winters? How IP67 sealing, minus 40 cold ratings and aluminum track handle snow, ice dams and freeze-thaw cycles.
summary: Yes, properly built permanent outdoor lights are designed for Ontario winters: quality systems use IP67 sealed LEDs, components cold-rated to minus 40 degrees Celsius, UV-rated cable and aluminum track that does not crack in the cold. Mounting under or on the soffit and fascia keeps the lights out of the worst snow load and ice, so they can stay up and keep working all year.
keyTakeaways: IP67 sealing means the LEDs are protected against dust and against temporary immersion in water, which covers rain, snowmelt and ice.
Components cold-rated to minus 40 degrees Celsius handle even the coldest Southwestern Ontario nights.
Aluminum track resists cracking and sagging through repeated freeze-thaw cycles.
Mounting on the soffit or fascia keeps the lights below snow sitting on the roof and away from shovels and roof rakes.
LEDs actually run more efficiently in cold weather, so winter is not hard on the light source itself.

sections.heading: What Ontario Winters Throw at Exterior Lighting
paragraphs: Southwestern Ontario winters are not just cold; they are changeable. London and the communities north and west of it sit in a snowbelt fed by lake-effect snow off Lake Huron, which can drop heavy, wet bands of snow in a matter of hours. Kitchener-Waterloo, Guelph and Stratford see similar storms, while the whole region swings above and below freezing many times between December and March.

Those freeze-thaw cycles are the real test. Water gets into any gap, freezes, expands and pries things apart, then melts and repeats. Cheap plastic housings become brittle, seals fail, and moisture reaches the electronics. Wind-driven sleet and road salt carried on spray near driveways add to the stress. Any lighting meant to stay up year-round has to be built with all of this in mind.

sections.heading: IP67 Sealing and Why It Matters
paragraphs: The IP rating system describes how well an enclosure keeps out solids and water. The first digit, 6, means fully dust-tight. The second digit, 7, means the device is protected against temporary immersion in water. For roofline lighting, that level of protection covers driving rain, snowmelt running along the trim and water that sits on the fixture before refreezing. It is the level of protection a permanent system needs.

Many decorative string lights sold for seasonal use carry lower ratings intended for occasional outdoor exposure. That is fine for six weeks in December, but not for twelve months a year, every year. Our LEDs are IP67 sealed, and connections between sections are weatherproofed so moisture cannot track along the cable into the nodes. Those details are what separate a permanent system from a temporary one that happens to be left up.

sections.heading: Cold Ratings Down to Minus 40 Degrees Celsius
paragraphs: Our components are cold-rated to minus 40 degrees Celsius, which is colder than Southwestern Ontario typically gets. Even the deep cold snaps that push Woodstock or Tillsonburg into the minus 20s and occasionally the minus 30s with windchill sit well within that range. Cold rating matters for the cable jackets, seals and solder joints, which can crack or lose flexibility if they are not designed for it.

The LEDs themselves actually like the cold. Heat is the main enemy of LED lifespan, so winter operation tends to be easy on the light source. The 50,000 plus hour rated life applies to year-round use, and cold nights in January are among the most comfortable operating conditions the LEDs will see. Long winter nights simply mean more time to enjoy them.

sections.heading: Snow Load, Ice Dams and Roof Raking
paragraphs: Snow sits on the roof surface, not under the soffit. Because the track mounts in the soffit or fascia channel, the lights stay below and outside the snow load, rather than being buried the way clip-on shingle lights can be. Light continues to wash the roofline even when the roof itself is covered. Melting snow simply drips past the track rather than burying it.

Ice dams form at the eaves when heat escaping from the attic melts snow that refreezes at the colder overhang. Permanent lighting does not cause ice dams, and it is mounted below the area where they form. Homeowners who use a roof rake to pull snow off the lower edge can do so without catching clips or strings, which is a common way seasonal lights get torn down mid-winter.
bullets: Lights mount below the snow, not on the shingles
No clips for roof rakes or ice to pull loose
Track stays rigid under icicle weight
Gutters remain accessible for clearing

sections.heading: Freeze-Thaw, Summer Sun and the Rest of the Year
paragraphs: Aluminum track handles temperature swings without cracking, and it is not affected by the brittleness that plastic housings develop after a few winters. Mounting hardware is designed to hold firm as the house trim expands and contracts across the seasons. That stability keeps runs straight and joints tight, which in turn keeps water out. There are no plastic clips to snap in the cold.

Ontario summers bring their own stress: strong UV exposure on south- and west-facing elevations, heat on dark trim and heavy thunderstorms. The cable used is UV-rated so it does not chalk or crack in the sun, and the IP67 sealing that protects against snowmelt also protects against summer downpours. A system that survives Ontario's full calendar is the standard to expect.

sections.heading: What to Do During and After a Winter Storm
paragraphs: In most cases, nothing. You do not need to turn the lights off for snow, rain or cold. If a storm causes a power outage, the controller restarts when power returns and resumes its schedule. You may want to check the app after a long outage to confirm the system reconnected to Wi-Fi. Schedules then carry on exactly as before.

If heavy icicles form directly on the track, let them melt naturally rather than knocking them off with a shovel or broom, which is more likely to damage trim than the lights. If anything ever stops working after a storm, our lifetime warranty on parts, hardware and workmanship covers the repair, and we respond within 24 hours at 519-266-6796. We would rather hear about it early.

faqs.question: Do I need to take permanent lights down for winter?
faqs.answer: No. Permanent systems are designed to stay installed all year. The LEDs are IP67 sealed, components are cold-rated to minus 40 degrees Celsius and the aluminum track handles freeze-thaw cycles. Winter is actually the season most owners use them most, for Christmas and New Year scenes.

faqs.question: Will snow cover the lights?
faqs.answer: Snow builds up on the roof surface, while permanent lights mount on the soffit or fascia below the roof edge. That keeps them clear of snow load in most conditions, so they continue to light the roofline even during heavy lake-effect snow events.

faqs.question: Can ice damage permanent lights?
faqs.answer: Sealed IP67 LEDs and aluminum track are built to handle ice and meltwater. The risk usually comes from people chipping ice off with tools rather than the ice itself. Let icicles melt naturally, and if anything is damaged the lifetime warranty covers parts, hardware and workmanship.

title: The Best Colours and Scenes for Every Holiday and Occasion
metaTitle: Best Permanent Light Colours for Every Holiday
metaDescription: The best permanent lighting colours and scenes for every holiday in Ontario, from Christmas and Halloween to Canada Day, Diwali, game nights and birthdays.
summary: The best permanent lighting scenes use two or three colours tied to the occasion, moderate brightness and slow or gentle motion, such as warm white with red accents for Christmas, orange and purple for Halloween, and red and white for Canada Day. Saving a scene for each holiday and scheduling it in the app means your roofline changes automatically through the year.
keyTakeaways: Two or three colours almost always look better from the street than a full rainbow.
Slow fades, gentle twinkles and static patterns look more refined than fast chases for everyday use.
Warm white is the best default for non-holiday evenings and adds curb appeal and security lighting.
Building a calendar of scenes in the app once means the lights change for each holiday without any effort.
Brightness around 40 to 70 percent is usually plenty for residential streets and avoids glare for neighbours.

sections.heading: Design Principles for Great-Looking Roofline Scenes
paragraphs: With more than 16 million colours available, the temptation is to use all of them. The houses that look best from the street usually do the opposite. Pick two or three colours that clearly signal the occasion, repeat them in an even pattern and let the architecture of the house do the rest. A simple red and white alternating pattern reads instantly as Canada Day from a block away; a rainbow chase reads as noise.

Motion should be used with restraint. A slow fade, a gentle twinkle or a pattern that drifts along the roofline over several seconds feels festive and calm. Fast strobes and rapid chases are fun for a party or a big game but can be tiring to look at night after night and may bother neighbours. Brightness follows the same rule: start around half and adjust from the street.
bullets: Use two or three colours per scene
Favour slow fades and twinkles over fast effects
Start at about 50 percent brightness and adjust from the street
Keep a warm white scene as your everyday default

sections.heading: Christmas and Winter Holiday Scenes
paragraphs: Christmas is where most homeowners start. Classic choices include a warm white outline that mimics traditional incandescent strings, red and green alternating in groups of three or four LEDs, a multicolour pattern that recalls old C9 bulbs, and a cool white with a slow twinkle that suggests falling snow. Running a warm white base with red accents at the peaks is a refined option that pairs well with wreaths and garland.

For Hanukkah, blue and white in a gentle alternating pattern is the standard choice, and some families add a slow build across eight segments of the roofline. New Year's Eve suits gold and white with a subtle sparkle, switched to a celebratory animation for the countdown. After the holidays, a soft ice blue and white scene can carry the house through the darker weeks of January.

sections.heading: Halloween, Thanksgiving and Autumn Scenes
paragraphs: Halloween is the second most popular holiday for permanent lighting in Ontario. Orange and purple alternating is the go-to, with green added for a slightly spookier palette. A slow flicker or random sparkle in orange can mimic candlelight in jack-o'-lanterns, and a deep red pulse works for houses that go all out on October 31. Schedule it for the last week or two of October so the change feels like an event.

For Thanksgiving in early October, warm amber, gold and deep orange in a static pattern complement autumn wreaths and mums without feeling like Halloween arrived early. Through the rest of fall, a warm white set slightly lower in brightness keeps the house welcoming as the evenings get shorter and the clocks change in November. A dimmer setting also suits early evenings.

sections.heading: Canada Day, Victoria Day and Summer Celebrations
paragraphs: Red and white is the obvious Canada Day scene, and it looks best as clean blocks of colour rather than single alternating LEDs, which can blend into pink from a distance. Try groups of five or six LEDs per colour. A slow wave moving along the roofline adds energy for the evening of July 1 when neighbours are out for fireworks. Victoria Day can borrow the same scene or use a softer white and gold.

Summer is also prime time for backyard entertaining. If you have a rear zone, set warm white or a soft amber over the patio for barbecues and evening fires, and switch to a party scene with brighter colours for birthdays and graduations. Because the zones are independent, the front can stay understated while the back has more fun. That is one of the main benefits of zones.

sections.heading: Cultural Festivals, Sports and Personal Occasions
paragraphs: Southwestern Ontario is home to families celebrating many traditions, and permanent lighting adapts to all of them. Diwali scenes often use warm gold, saffron and deep pink with a gentle shimmer that evokes rows of diyas. Eid celebrations commonly use white and gold or green and white. Lunar New Year suits red and gold. Saving these as named scenes makes them easy to schedule year after year.

Sports fans can set team colours for game days and playoff runs, whether that is a local hockey club or a national team. Personal occasions work too: pink or blue for a new baby, a birthday scene in the guest of honour's favourite colours, or teal and white for an awareness month that matters to your family. These are the moments that make the system feel personal.

sections.heading: Building a Year-Round Lighting Calendar in the App
paragraphs: The easiest way to enjoy all of this is to set it once. In the app, create a scene for each occasion you care about, then build schedules with start and end dates and on and off times. For example, warm white from dusk to midnight as the default, Halloween from October 24 to 31, Christmas from late November to early January, and Canada Day for the weekend around July 1.

Once the calendar is in place, the lights change automatically, and you only open the app when you want something special. During installation we set up starter scenes and a basic schedule and show you how to adjust them. If you want help designing a calendar for your household, call 519-266-6796 and we can walk you through it. It usually takes only a few minutes.

faqs.question: What is the best everyday colour for permanent lights?
faqs.answer: Warm white is the most popular everyday choice. It highlights the roofline, lights the driveway and entry, and looks like architectural accent lighting rather than a decoration. Running it at moderate brightness from dusk to around midnight gives curb appeal and a sense of security without glare.

faqs.question: Can I set different holidays to change automatically?
faqs.answer: Yes. The app lets you save scenes and schedule them by date and time, so Halloween, Christmas, Canada Day and other occasions switch on and off on their own. You can still override the schedule from your phone at any time for a party or special event.

faqs.question: Why does my red and white scene look pink from the street?
faqs.answer: When single LEDs alternate between red and white, the colours blend together at a distance. Grouping five or six LEDs per colour keeps each block distinct, so the pattern reads clearly as red and white from across the street. The same trick helps with other two-colour holiday scenes.

title: Does Permanent Lighting Add Home Value? Curb Appeal, Security, Resale
metaTitle: Does Permanent Lighting Add Home Value?
metaDescription: Does permanent lighting add home value in Ontario? How permanent roofline lights affect curb appeal, listing photos, home security and resale for homeowners.
summary: Permanent lighting is best thought of as a curb appeal and lifestyle upgrade rather than a guaranteed dollar-for-dollar increase in appraised value, but it can make a home more memorable to buyers, improve evening listing photos and add useful security lighting. Its value to you depends on how long you stay, how much you use it and how cleanly it is installed.
keyTakeaways: Appraisers generally do not assign a fixed value to exterior lighting, so treat permanent lights as a curb appeal investment rather than a guaranteed return.
Well-installed, colour-matched systems help a home stand out in twilight listing photos and showings.
Scheduled warm white lighting around the roofline improves visibility of entries, driveways and yards at night.
A transferable warranty and clear documentation make the system an easier selling feature.
Poorly installed or obviously visible systems can work against curb appeal, so installation quality matters.

sections.heading: How Appraisers and Buyers View Exterior Lighting
paragraphs: It helps to be realistic. In Ontario, residential appraisals lean heavily on comparable sales, square footage, location, lot size and the condition of major systems like the roof, furnace and windows. Exterior lighting rarely appears as its own line item, and no one can promise that a $5,000 lighting system will add exactly $5,000 to an appraised value. Anyone claiming a guaranteed return is overselling.

Buyers are a different story. They make emotional decisions, often within seconds of seeing a listing photo or pulling into the driveway. Features that make a home feel finished, cared for and a little special can influence which homes make the shortlist and how competitive offers become. Permanent lighting falls into that category of upgrades, alongside landscaping, a refreshed front door and good exterior trim.

sections.heading: Curb Appeal Every Night of the Year
paragraphs: Most exterior upgrades only show during the day. Permanent roofline lighting adds an evening layer. A soft warm white outline along the soffits defines the architecture of the house, highlights peaks and gables, and makes the home look intentional after dark, which in Southwestern Ontario is a lot of hours from November through February. That added evening presence is something seasonal lights only offer for a few weeks a year.

Because the track is colour-matched to your soffit or fascia, the daytime appearance stays clean, so you do not trade daytime curb appeal for night-time impact. That combination is why permanent lighting suits homes in established neighbourhoods in London, Guelph and Cambridge as well as newer builds in Woodstock, Ingersoll and St. Thomas, where many houses on a street look similar.

sections.heading: Twilight Listing Photos and Showings
paragraphs: Real estate photographers often shoot a twilight exterior for higher-end listings, because a glowing house against a deep blue sky stands out in online search results. Permanent lighting gives the photographer an evenly lit roofline to work with, rather than relying on interior lights alone. The result is a hero image that is more likely to catch a scrolling buyer's attention.

For evening showings in fall and winter, scheduled warm white lighting helps buyers see the property clearly and safely as they arrive. It is a small detail, but walking up to a well-lit, welcoming home after dark feels different from arriving at a dim one, and first impressions shape how buyers view everything inside. Agents often note that the first photo largely decides whether a buyer clicks through.

sections.heading: Security and Safety Benefits of Roofline Lighting
paragraphs: Light around the perimeter of a house is a simple, widely recommended deterrent, because it removes the dark corners where someone could approach unseen. Permanent lighting runs along the eaves, so it can wash the driveway, front walkway, side yards and backyard depending on which zones you install. A schedule that turns on warm white at sunset every day means the home never sits dark, even when you are away.

There are everyday safety benefits too. Better visibility of steps, walkways and icy driveways reduces slips during winter evenings. You can also brighten a zone from your phone if you hear something outside or are arriving home late. While we would never present lighting as a complete security system, it is a practical layer that complements cameras and locks. It is lighting you will use every night.
bullets: Dusk-to-midnight schedules keep the property lit when you are away
Perimeter zones light side yards and backyards, not just the front
Brighter lighting on demand from your phone
Improved visibility of icy walkways and steps

sections.heading: What Makes Permanent Lighting a Selling Feature
paragraphs: To turn lighting into an asset at sale time, a few things matter. First, the installation needs to look clean in daylight, with colour-matched track, straight runs and hidden cable. Second, the system should be working and easy to hand over, with the controller reset and the new owners shown how to download the app. Third, buyers want to know it is covered.

Our lifetime warranty on parts, hardware and workmanship gives you something concrete to put in a listing feature sheet. Keep your installation paperwork and warranty details with your other home documents. Your agent can mention it alongside other upgrades, and a buyer touring in November or December will see the system at its best. Clear paperwork builds buyer confidence.

sections.heading: When Permanent Lighting Makes the Most Sense
paragraphs: If you plan to stay in your home for five years or more, permanent lighting usually pays back through avoided seasonal installation costs, year-round enjoyment and security lighting, with any resale appeal as a bonus. If you are selling in the next few months, other preparation such as painting, landscaping and decluttering will typically produce more return per dollar. Timing makes a real difference.

If you are in between, a phased approach can work: light the front elevation now for immediate curb appeal and add the rest later. Our free AI Home Preview shows how your house would look with permanent lighting, emailed within one business day, which can help you decide whether the look suits your home. There is no charge and no obligation.

faqs.question: Will permanent lights increase my home's appraised value?
faqs.answer: Appraisals in Ontario rely mainly on comparable sales, size, location and condition, so exterior lighting is not usually assigned a specific dollar value. Permanent lights are better viewed as a curb appeal upgrade that can make your home more attractive to buyers rather than a guaranteed appraisal increase.

faqs.question: Does the warranty transfer if I sell my house?
faqs.answer: Ask your installer to confirm warranty terms in writing. Our lifetime warranty covers parts, hardware and workmanship on the installation, and keeping the paperwork with your home documents makes it easy to present to buyers. Contact us before listing and we can confirm details for your specific system.

faqs.question: Can permanent lighting hurt curb appeal?
faqs.answer: It can if it is installed poorly. Generic white track on dark trim, crooked runs, exposed cable or overly bright flashing scenes can make a home look cluttered. Colour-matched track, careful installation and tasteful warm white everyday scenes avoid those problems.

title: Controlling Permanent Lights From Your Phone: Scenes, Schedules, Zones
metaTitle: Permanent Lighting App Control: Scenes and Zones
metaDescription: A practical guide to permanent lighting app control for Ontario homes: building scenes, setting schedules and timers, splitting zones and sharing access.
summary: Permanent lights are controlled from a phone app that connects to a controller on your home Wi-Fi, letting you choose colours, save scenes, set schedules and timers, and run different parts of the house as separate zones. Most owners set up a year-round schedule once and then only open the app for parties, holidays or one-off changes.
keyTakeaways: Scenes save a combination of colours, pattern, motion and brightness so you can recall them with one tap.
Schedules switch scenes on and off automatically by time, date or around sunset.
Zones let the front, sides, garage and backyard run different scenes or be turned off independently.
Timers are handy for one-off events, such as lighting the backyard for three hours during a party.
A strong Wi-Fi signal at the controller location is the most important factor in reliable app control.

sections.heading: How the App Connects to Your Lights
paragraphs: The controller is a small, weatherproof box installed near the power supply, typically in the garage, attic space or on an exterior wall near an outlet. It joins your home Wi-Fi network and receives instructions from the app on your phone. When you tap a scene, the app sends it to the controller, which then sends data down the LED run telling each individually addressable LED what colour and brightness to show.

Because the controller stores scenes and schedules locally, the lights keep following their programmed routine even if your internet connection drops for a while. During installation we pair the controller with your network, confirm signal strength at its location and install the app on your phone so everything works before the crew leaves. You leave with a working system and a phone that already controls it.

sections.heading: Creating and Saving Scenes
paragraphs: A scene is a saved look. It combines colours, a pattern such as solid, alternating, gradient or twinkle, any motion and speed, and a brightness level. Most apps include a library of preset scenes for popular holidays, which are a good starting point. You can tweak a preset and save it under your own name, or build one from scratch by selecting colours and painting them along the roofline.

Name scenes clearly so they are easy to find later, for example Everyday Warm White, Christmas Classic, Halloween Spooky or Canada Day Wave. Many households end up with eight to fifteen scenes they actually use. Test new scenes from the street rather than the front step, since brightness and colour mix look different at a distance. You can always edit or rename scenes later.
bullets: Start from a preset and adjust colours to suit your trim
Group LEDs in blocks of several for two-colour patterns
Keep motion slow for everyday use
Check every new scene from across the street

sections.heading: Schedules, Sunset Triggers and Timers
paragraphs: Schedules are what make permanent lighting effortless. A typical setup turns on Everyday Warm White at sunset and off at midnight every night. Sunset-based scheduling adjusts automatically through the year, which matters in Ontario where sunset moves from around 4:45 p.m. in December to around 9:00 p.m. in late June. Fixed clock times would leave the lights on in daylight in summer or late to start in winter.

Date-based schedules then layer holiday scenes on top. Halloween can run for the last week of October, Christmas from the end of November into early January and Canada Day over the long weekend. Timers handle one-off needs, such as lighting the backyard zone for three hours during a barbecue or switching to a birthday scene until 10 p.m. before returning to the normal schedule.

sections.heading: Setting Up Zones Around the House
paragraphs: Zones divide the system into sections that can be controlled independently. Common layouts include a front zone for the main street-facing roofline, side zones, a backyard zone and a separate zone for a detached garage or shop. Zones are planned during the quote and installation, since each one needs its own data run from the controller. Most homes use two to four zones.

Zones open up practical and creative options. You might keep the front in warm white for curb appeal while the backyard runs a brighter scene for a party, or switch off the zone outside a bedroom window while leaving the rest on. You can also sync all zones together for a big holiday display so the roofline acts as one continuous canvas.

sections.heading: Sharing Access and Everyday Tips
paragraphs: Most households want more than one person to be able to control the lights. Ask during setup how to add additional family members' phones so everyone has access without sharing passwords. If you have teenagers, you may want to agree on house rules for brightness and late-night disco scenes before the neighbours have an opinion about it. Shared access also keeps one person from becoming the household lighting technician.

A few habits keep things simple. Keep the app updated, since updates can add effects and improve reliability. If you change your Wi-Fi router or password, the controller will need to rejoin the new network, so plan for that when switching internet providers. And if a scene ever looks wrong, try power-cycling the controller before assuming anything is broken. That solves most glitches.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting Common App Issues
paragraphs: Most app problems come down to Wi-Fi. If the app says the controller is offline, check that your router is working and that the controller location still has a good signal. Garages and attics with thick walls or foil-faced insulation can weaken Wi-Fi, and a mesh node or extender nearby usually solves it. After a power outage, give the controller a minute or two to reconnect.

If a section of lights shows the wrong colour or does not light while the rest of the run is fine, note where it starts and contact us. Our lifetime warranty covers parts, hardware and workmanship, and we respond within 24 hours. You can reach us at 519-266-6796 and we can often diagnose the issue over the phone. Most issues are quick to resolve.

faqs.question: Do I need Wi-Fi to control permanent lights?
faqs.answer: Yes, the controller connects to your home Wi-Fi so the app can send it new scenes and schedules. Saved schedules generally run from the controller itself, so the lights keep working during a short internet outage. A good signal at the controller location is important for reliable control.

faqs.question: Can permanent lights turn on automatically at sunset?
faqs.answer: Yes. Sunset-based schedules adjust daily to match the changing sunset time in Ontario, so the lights come on at dusk in both December and June without you changing anything. You can set a fixed off time such as midnight or a set number of hours after sunset.

faqs.question: How many people can control the lights?
faqs.answer: Multiple household members can usually install the app and control the system. We set up the primary account during installation and can show you how to add family members so everyone can change scenes, adjust brightness or switch zones from their own phones.

title: Permanent Lighting Warranty and Maintenance: What Actually Needs Doing
metaDescription: Permanent lighting warranty and maintenance in Ontario explained: what a lifetime warranty should cover, simple yearly checks and what to do if an LED fails.
summary: Permanent lighting needs very little maintenance: an occasional visual check, keeping the controller's Wi-Fi connection healthy and gently rinsing the track if it gets dirty is usually all that is required. A strong warranty, such as a lifetime warranty on parts, hardware and workmanship, should cover the rest, including repairs if an LED section or the controller ever fails.
keyTakeaways: Rated at 50,000 plus hours, the LEDs are designed to last many years of nightly use.
Routine maintenance is limited to a quick visual check, light cleaning and keeping the app and Wi-Fi up to date.
A good warranty covers parts, hardware and workmanship, not just the LEDs themselves.
Roof, gutter and soffit work by other trades is the most common cause of accidental damage, so plan for it.
Get warranty terms in writing and keep them with your home documents.

sections.heading: What a Permanent Lighting Warranty Should Cover
paragraphs: Warranties in this industry vary a lot, so read the fine print. Some cover only the LEDs for a few years, others separate parts and labour, and some exclude the controller or power supply. Our systems carry a lifetime warranty on parts, hardware and workmanship, which means the LEDs, track, cable, connectors, controller, power supply and the quality of the installation itself are all included.

Workmanship coverage matters as much as product coverage. If a joint was not sealed properly or a run was mounted incorrectly, the problem is installation rather than a faulty LED, and a parts-only warranty would leave you paying for the service call. When comparing installers, ask exactly what is covered, for how long, who performs the repairs and how quickly they respond.
bullets: LEDs, track, cable and connectors
Controller and power supply
Installation workmanship, including sealing and mounting
Labour to diagnose and repair covered issues

sections.heading: How Long Permanent LEDs Last
paragraphs: Our LEDs are rated for 50,000 plus hours of operation. To put that in context, running the lights six hours every single night adds up to about 2,190 hours a year, so the rated life works out to well over twenty years of nightly use. Most homeowners run their lights fewer hours than that, particularly in summer when sunset is late.

LED life is affected most by heat and by how hard the LEDs are driven. Running scenes at moderate brightness rather than full power, which most people prefer for appearance anyway, is gentle on the components. Southwestern Ontario's cool climate also helps, since cold weather is easy on LEDs. Like any electronic product, individual failures can still happen, which is what the warranty is for.

sections.heading: Simple Yearly Maintenance Checklist
paragraphs: There is no annual service visit required. Once or twice a year, ideally in spring after the snow melts and again in early fall before the holiday season, run a bright white scene at dusk and walk around the house. Look for any section that is dim, the wrong colour or not lit, and check that the track is straight and secure after winter.

If the track looks dusty or has spider webs, which is common under soffits, a gentle rinse with a garden hose or a soft brush with mild soapy water is enough. Avoid pressure washers aimed directly at the track or connections. Keep the app updated, and confirm the controller is still online if you have changed your router or internet provider.

sections.heading: Working Around Roofers, Gutter Installers and Painters
paragraphs: The most common cause of damage to permanent lighting is not weather; it is other work on the house. Roof replacements, new gutters, eavestrough cleaning, soffit or fascia replacement and exterior painting all happen right where the lights are mounted. A crew that does not know the lights are there can step on cable, pry the track or paint over it.

Before any exterior work, let the contractor know about the lighting and contact us. In many cases sections can be carefully removed and reinstalled, or the crew simply works around them. Damage caused by third parties is generally outside any warranty, so a short phone call beforehand can save a repair bill afterwards. Reinstallation can usually be scheduled quickly once the other work is finished.

sections.heading: What to Do If a Light or Section Stops Working
paragraphs: Start with the basics. Check that the outlet or breaker feeding the power supply has not tripped, since exterior GFCI outlets can trip during heavy rain or when other devices share the circuit. Power-cycle the controller by unplugging it for thirty seconds. Confirm the app shows the controller online. Many apparent failures are resolved by one of these steps. Note the outlet location in advance.

If one section is out or showing the wrong colour while the rest works, note where the problem starts and send a photo or video. Because the system is modular and housed in track, the affected section can be replaced without taking down the whole run. Call 519-266-6796; we respond within 24 hours and covered repairs are handled under the lifetime warranty.

sections.heading: Comparing Maintenance With Seasonal Christmas Lights
paragraphs: Seasonal lights require a full cycle of work every year: testing strings, replacing burnt-out bulbs, hanging, adjusting clips after storms, taking down in January, untangling and storing. Even when a professional does the work, it still has to be booked and paid for each season, and plastic clips and wire jackets degrade from repeated handling. Bulbs also burn out and need replacing.

Permanent lighting removes that cycle. The system stays sealed in its track, is not handled every year and does not need storage space in the garage or basement. For many Ontario homeowners, that reduction in hassle is as much a reason to switch as the colour options. It also frees up storage space in the garage or basement that boxes of tangled strings, clips and extension cords used to take over. Many owners say the time saved each November and January was what convinced them.

faqs.question: Do permanent lights need to be cleaned?
faqs.answer: Only occasionally. Under-soffit track tends to stay fairly clean, but dust and spider webs can build up. A gentle rinse with a garden hose or a soft brush with mild soapy water once a year is usually enough. Avoid aiming a pressure washer directly at the track and connections.

faqs.question: What does a lifetime warranty on permanent lighting include?
faqs.answer: Ours covers parts, hardware and workmanship. That includes the LEDs, track, cable, connectors, controller, power supply and the quality of the installation. Warranties differ between companies, so always ask what is covered, who performs repairs and how quickly they respond.

faqs.question: Will my lights be damaged if I replace my roof or gutters?

metaDescription: How to choose a permanent lighting installer in Ontario: 12 questions to ask about warranty, LEDs, colour-matching, electrical work, insurance and pricing.
summary: To choose a permanent lighting installer in Ontario, compare written quotes on the same footage and ask specific questions about the LEDs, track colour-matching, weather ratings, warranty coverage, electrical work, insurance and post-install support. The best installers will answer in writing, show you daytime and night-time examples, and let you see the product on your own house before you pay.

Ask whether LEDs are individually addressable RGBW and what weather and cold ratings they carry.

Any new outlet or circuit should be handled by a licensed electrical contractor with ESA notification.
Seeing a live sample on your own house is the most reliable way to judge quality before committing.

sections.heading: Why Installer Choice Matters More Than the Brand Name
paragraphs: Permanent lighting is a product and a trade at the same time. Two companies can buy similar LEDs and still deliver very different results, because the finished look depends on how the track is matched, measured, cut, joined and mounted, and how the cabling and controller are hidden. The installer also determines how quickly problems get fixed years from now.

The industry has grown quickly, and Southwestern Ontario now has a mix of dedicated lighting companies, seasonal light installers adding permanent systems and general contractors offering it as a sideline. Asking the right questions helps separate experienced specialists from crews learning on your house. The twelve questions below are grouped by topic so you can work through them with each company you are considering.

sections.heading: Questions About the Product: LEDs, Track and Ratings
paragraphs: Start with the hardware, because it determines what the system can do. Individually addressable LEDs allow patterns and per-light colour control; non-addressable strips show one colour along the whole run. A dedicated white channel, as in RGBW, produces a far better everyday white than RGB alone. Weather and cold ratings tell you whether the system was designed for Canadian winters or for milder climates.

Ask about the track too. Aluminum holds its shape through freeze-thaw cycles better than plastic, and genuine colour-matching to your soffit or fascia is the difference between a system that disappears in daylight and one that looks like an afterthought. Ask to see a physical sample of the track and an LED node so you can judge the build quality for yourself, and ask whether the installer will match your actual trim colour or offer only a few stock finishes.

4. What is the rated LED life in hours?

sections.heading: Questions About Installation and Electrical Work
paragraphs: Installation methods vary. Ask whether anything will penetrate the roof, since mounting through shingles can create leak points and affect roofing warranties. Systems that clip into the soffit or fascia channel avoid that. Ask how long the install takes, how corners and peaks are handled, and where the controller and power supply will live. Clear answers here show experience.

Electrical work deserves particular attention. Most systems plug into an existing exterior GFCI outlet, but if a new outlet or circuit is needed, that work must be done by a licensed electrical contractor under the Ontario Electrical Safety Code, with notification to the Electrical Safety Authority. Be wary of any company that suggests skipping this or having an unlicensed crew member wire it in.

6. How long will installation take, and where will the controller and power supply go?
7. If electrical work is needed, who does it and will it be ESA-notified?

sections.heading: Questions About Warranty, Support and the App
paragraphs: Warranty language is where quotes that look similar often differ. Some cover LEDs only, some cover parts but not labour, and some exclude the controller. Ask for the full terms in writing. Our own systems carry a lifetime warranty on parts, hardware and workmanship, which is the standard we would encourage you to compare against. Anything less should be priced accordingly.

Support matters just as much. Ask who you call if something stops working, how fast they respond and whether they are local enough to come out quickly. Ask about the app as well: is there a subscription fee, can multiple family members use it, and will the installer set up scenes and schedules and show you how it works before leaving.

10. Who handles service calls, and how quickly do you respond?

sections.heading: Questions About Price and Proof
paragraphs: Quotes should list lit footage, number of zones, what is included and any electrical or access charges. Comparing price per lit foot across quotes helps you spot outliers. A quote far below others often leaves out the controller, colour-matching, a proper warranty or labour that appears later as an extra. Ask each company to itemize so you can compare line by line, and make sure the footage they measured matches the runs you actually want lit.

Finally, ask for proof. Photos taken in daylight show whether track blends in; night photos show colour quality and evenness. The strongest proof is seeing the product on your own home. That is why we offer a free on-site demo, mounting a colour-matched live sample section on your house and lighting it at night before you pay anything. It removes the guesswork.
bullets: 12. Can I see the product, colour-matched and lit, on my own house before I commit?

sections.heading: Red Flags When Comparing Permanent Lighting Companies
paragraphs: Watch for high-pressure tactics such as one-day-only pricing, large non-refundable deposits before a site visit, or vague answers about what brand of LEDs and controller you are getting. Be cautious of quotes delivered without anyone measuring the roofline, since footage estimates from satellite images often miss peaks and returns. An accurate quote should come from someone who has walked around your home, looked at the soffit and fascia, and checked where power and the controller will go.

Also watch for warranties that are only verbal, installers who cannot say who will service the system next year, and portfolios that show only night photos. A reputable installer in Ontario should be comfortable putting everything in writing, answering every one of the twelve questions above and responding promptly. We reply within 24 hours at 519-266-6796. Take your time.

faqs.question: Should I get more than one quote for permanent lighting?
faqs.answer: Yes. Getting two or three written quotes for the same lit footage and zones makes it easier to compare price per foot, warranty coverage and included components. Make sure each quote is based on an actual measurement of your roofline rather than a rough estimate from photos.

faqs.question: Does a permanent lighting installer need to be an electrician?
faqs.answer: Plugging a low-voltage system into an existing exterior outlet does not require an electrician. Adding a new outlet or circuit does, and in Ontario that work must be done by a licensed electrical contractor with ESA notification. Ask each installer how they handle electrical work.

faqs.question: How long should a permanent lighting warranty be?
faqs.answer: Look for long coverage that includes parts, hardware and workmanship rather than LEDs alone. We offer a lifetime warranty on all three. Whatever the term, make sure it is in writing and that you know who performs repairs and how quickly they respond.

That means the key questions are what your soffit and fascia are made of, what condition they are in, how deep the overhang is and where the eavestrough sits. sections.heading: Aluminum and Vinyl Soffit: The Most Common Ontario Setup
paragraphs: Most houses built or re-trimmed in Ontario over the last few decades have aluminum fascia wrap and either aluminum or vinyl vented soffit. These materials are excellent for permanent lighting. They provide a consistent, straight surface, they do not rot, and the track can be colour-matched to the factory trim colour so it blends in. It is the simplest scenario.

Vented soffit panels are designed to let air into the attic, and the track does not block that ventilation in any meaningful way because it is slim and runs along the outer edge. If any panels are loose or have been pushed up by wind or animals, we secure them as part of the install so the track has a solid base.

sections.heading: Wood Soffit and Fascia on Older Homes
paragraphs: Older homes in places like St. Thomas, Stratford and Brantford often still have painted wood soffit and fascia. Sound wood is a perfectly good mounting surface, and the track can be colour-matched to the paint. The concern is condition: wood that is soft, cracked or rotted from years of ice dams and leaking eavestroughs will not hold fasteners well. Condition is easy to check.

During the on-site visit we check the trim along the planned runs. If we find damage, we will point it out so you can have it repaired or wrapped in aluminum before installation. Fixing it first avoids having to remove and reinstall lights later, and it protects the house from further water damage at the same time. Better trim makes for a better install.

sections.heading: Brick, Stone and Stucco Homes
paragraphs: Brick and stone are extremely common in Southwestern Ontario, and stucco appears on many custom and newer homes. Because the lights follow the roof trim, these wall finishes are not drilled or affected. The light washes down from the overhang and can actually look particularly striking on textured masonry, where it picks out the depth of the brick or stone.

Power and data cable are routed along trim lines and through the soffit or garage, so there is typically no need to run anything across the face of the masonry. If an exterior outlet needs to be added on a brick wall, a licensed electrician handles that under the Ontario Electrical Safety Code. The outlet is then fitted with a weatherproof in-use cover.

sections.heading: Unusual Rooflines, Gables and Overhangs
paragraphs: Not every house is a simple rectangle. Steep gables, dormers, hip roofs, turrets, porches and garages with different roof heights all add character and a few challenges. The track can follow rakes up to peaks and around inside and outside corners, and separate roof sections can be connected with tidy cable runs or set up as their own zones. Each roofline is laid out individually.

Homes with very shallow or no overhang can usually be lit by mounting on the face of the fascia. The look is a slightly crisper outline from the street. Our free on-site demo is the best way to confirm compatibility, since we colour-match your trim and mount a live sample section exactly where the system would go, then light it at night.

faqs.answer: Yes. Permanent lights mount to the soffit or fascia of the roof overhang, not to the brick itself, so masonry walls are not drilled or affected. The light washes down from the roofline and often highlights the texture of brick or stone nicely at night.

faqs.question: Will permanent lighting damage my vinyl soffit?
faqs.answer: No, when installed properly. The track mounts securely without compromising the panels, and loose panels are fastened as part of the install. The slim track runs along the outer edge, so it does not meaningfully reduce attic ventilation through vented soffit.

sections.heading: What Makes C9 Lights the Classic Christmas Look
paragraphs: C9 refers to the bulb size: about 1.125 inches in diameter, larger than the C7 and much larger than mini lights. The size makes each bulb visible from a distance, producing the bold, evenly spaced outline that many people remember from childhood Christmases. Spaced along the eaves, peaks and garage roof, C9s give a home a strong, traditional silhouette. They suit almost any style of home.

Many families book C9 service year after year and are happy with it. summary: Permanent LED roofline lights use very little electricity: during typical scenes a residential system draws roughly as much as a few standard LED bulbs, which works out to an estimated $7 to $16 a year for nightly warm white use at Ontario rates of about $0.10 to $0.15 per kWh. sections.heading: How Much Power Permanent LED Lights Draw
paragraphs: LEDs are extremely efficient at turning electricity into light. A permanent roofline system on a typical Ontario home, with somewhere between 100 and 250 linear feet lit, draws roughly as much power as a few standard LED household bulbs during everyday scenes. Our estimate for a mid-sized home running warm white at moderate brightness is in the range of 30 to 60 watts.

Power draw rises with brightness and with how many colour channels each LED is using. A full-brightness white scene with every channel lit draws the most, while dim single-colour scenes draw the least. Because most homeowners run their lights at 40 to 70 percent brightness for appearance, everyday consumption sits toward the lower end. Actual figures depend on the length of the system and LED density.

sections.heading: Estimated Annual Running Costs in Ontario
paragraphs: Ontario electricity bills combine the energy charge with delivery, regulatory charges and HST, and rates vary by utility and by price plan, whether Hydro One or a local utility such as London Hydro or Enova Power. For a simple estimate, an all-in rate of about $0.10 to $0.15 per kWh is reasonable for planning. The table uses that range with the assumptions shown.

These figures are estimates, not guarantees. They assume a mid-sized residential system and typical use. Even if your system is larger or you run it longer, the numbers stay small compared with most household appliances, which is why power cost is rarely a deciding factor for homeowners. Your actual rate depends on your utility, price plan and usage, so check a recent bill if you want a more precise number for your home.

sections.heading: Comparing Permanent LEDs With Traditional Christmas Lights
paragraphs: The comparison with old-style lighting is striking. A single incandescent C9 bulb typically draws about 7 watts, so a 150-bulb roofline uses more than a kilowatt. Run for six hours a night over a 45-night holiday season, that is roughly 284 kWh, or an estimated $28 to $43 at Ontario rates, for one season of one holiday. And that is only the Christmas season.

A permanent LED system running every night of the year for everyday lighting typically uses less than half of that energy. LED C9 strings are also efficient, which is why most professional seasonal installations now use LED bulbs. If you still have boxes of incandescent strings in the basement, retiring them is one of the easiest ways to trim your December hydro bill.

sections.heading: Time-of-Use Rates and When Your Lights Run
paragraphs: Most Ontario residential customers are on time-of-use or tiered pricing, and some have chosen an ultra-low overnight plan. Under time-of-use, early evening hours on weekdays can fall in a higher-priced period, while later evenings, nights and weekends are cheaper. Because roofline lighting draws so little power, the difference between periods amounts to pennies per month. Scheduling is about habit more than savings.

If you want to optimize anyway, schedule everyday lights to turn off at a set time, such as 11 p.m. or midnight, rather than running all night. Sunset-based schedules in the app automatically shorten run time in summer, when sunset in Southwestern Ontario is after 9 p.m., and lengthen it in winter, when the lights do the most good. That keeps run time sensible all year.

sections.heading: Tips to Keep Permanent Lighting Costs Low
paragraphs: The most effective savings come from brightness and schedule. Running scenes at moderate brightness both looks better from the street and reduces power draw. Turning lights off overnight, using zones so only the elevations people actually see are lit on ordinary nights, and saving full-brightness white for special occasions all keep consumption minimal. None of these steps reduce what the system can do.

There is also a long-term angle. LEDs rated for 50,000 plus hours do not need replacement bulbs every season, and the system stays installed, so there are no annual installation fees. Combined with a lifetime warranty on parts, hardware and workmanship, electricity is effectively the only ongoing cost of ownership, and it is a small one. For most homes it amounts to a few dollars a month at most.

sections.heading: Do Permanent Lights Need a Dedicated Circuit?
paragraphs: Because power draw is so low, most residential systems plug into an existing exterior GFCI outlet without needing a new circuit. The power supply converts household 120-volt current to the low voltage the LEDs use. On larger homes or long runs, power may be fed at more than one point to keep colours consistent, which is a design matter rather than a load concern.

If an outlet needs to be added in a more convenient location, or a dedicated circuit is preferred, that work should be done by a licensed electrical contractor under the Ontario Electrical Safety Code with ESA notification. We identify any electrical needs during the free on-site demo, so they are clear in your quote before you commit. There are no hidden electrical surprises.

faqs.question: Will permanent lights raise my hydro bill much?
faqs.answer: Not noticeably for most homes. Our estimate for nightly warm white use on a typical Ontario home is $7 to $16 per year at $0.10 to $0.15 per kWh, with holiday scenes adding a few dollars per season. Actual cost depends on system size, brightness and run time.

faqs.question: Do brighter colours use more electricity?
faqs.answer: Yes. Power draw increases with brightness and with the number of colour channels each LED uses. Full-brightness white, which lights every channel, uses the most. Most homeowners run scenes at moderate brightness, which looks better and keeps power use low.

faqs.question: Are permanent LED lights more efficient than C9 Christmas lights?
faqs.answer: Permanent LEDs are far more efficient than incandescent C9 bulbs, which draw about 7 watts each. LED C9 bulbs are also efficient, so the gap is smaller there. The bigger advantage of permanent lighting is year-round use without annual installation costs.
